instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Phone Plan Upgrade
listeningScripts.text: Customer: Hi, I'm interested in upgrading my phone plan. I currently have the basic plan with 2 GB of data. Support: Great! I can definitely help with that. What's your phone number? Customer: It's 416-555-0234. I'm constantly hitting my data limit, especially with streaming videos. Support: I understand. Let me pull up your account. You're right, your basic plan is 2 GB per month at $35. What data usage would work better for you? Customer: Probably something like 10 GB. How much would that be? Support: We have a 10 GB plan at $65 per month. You'd also get unlimited texting and more calling minutes. Would that interest you? Customer: What's the difference in calling minutes from my current plan? Support: Your current plan has 200 minutes; the 10 GB plan has unlimited calling. Plus, there's no contract change required if you cancel later. Customer: Actually, do you have an 8 GB plan? That might be better value. Support: Good question. We do have an 8 GB plan at $55 per month with the same unlimited calling and texting. Customer: Perfect, I'll take that. When does it take effect? Support: I'm activating it right now. Your bill will reflect the change next billing cycle, which is on July 8th. The monthly cost goes from $35 to $55. Customer: That works for me. Thanks.

listeningScripts.title: Coffee Shop Catch-Up
listeningScripts.text: Sarah: Hey, how are you? It's been ages! Michael: I know, right? Must be like six months since we last hung out. Sarah: At least. How was your trip to Vancouver? Michael: It was amazing! The weather was beautiful, and I got to see the mountains every day. Sarah: That sounds incredible. Did you do any hiking? Michael: Yeah, we went up to Whistler for a weekend. The views were unbelievable. Sarah: I'm so jealous. I've been meaning to get out there. Hey, do you want to go grab dinner next week? Michael: Absolutely, I'd love that. How about Thursday? Sarah: Thursday works for me. There's that new Italian place downtown that opened last month. Michael: Perfect. Should we book a table? Sarah: Yeah, probably a good idea. What time? Michael: How about 7 PM? Sarah: Sounds good. I'll make the reservation.

listeningScripts.title: Public Transit New Route Announcement
listeningScripts.text: Good afternoon. Transit Authority is pleased to announce a new rapid bus route effective September 1st. The new Route 95 Express connects downtown to the northern suburbs, with stops at Central Station, City Hall, the Hospital, University Campus, and North Terminal. Service runs Monday through Friday from 6 AM to 10 PM, with departures every fifteen minutes during peak hours, 7 to 9 AM and 4 to 7 PM. Off-peak service is every thirty minutes. Weekend service begins December, with departures every twenty minutes from 9 AM to 8 PM. The Route 95 uses the new dedicated bus lane on Main Street, reducing travel time from downtown to North Terminal from forty-five minutes to approximately twenty-two minutes. Fares are the same as existing routes: single trip is three dollars fifty cents, and a monthly pass is ninety dollars. Seniors and students receive a twenty percent discount. The new buses feature USB charging ports, free Wi-Fi, and comfortable seating. Detailed schedules are available on our website and at all transit stations. Real-time tracking is available through our mobile app.

listeningScripts.title: BC Wildfire Season Begins Early
listeningScripts.text: British Columbia's wildfire season is beginning earlier than usual this year, prompting concerns among forest officials. As of June first, crews have already responded to 127 active fires across the province. The unusually warm and dry spring is blamed for the early start. The Ministry of Forests reports that conditions are expected to worsen through July and August. Last summer, the province experienced the worst fire season on record, with over 2.4 million hectares burned. This year's budget for firefighting has been increased to 560 million dollars, a 40 percent increase from the previous year. Communities at risk are being advised to prepare evacuation plans. The government is also deploying additional aerial firefighting resources, including five new helicopters equipped with water-dropping technology. Residents are reminded to clear dry vegetation from their properties and avoid open fires during high-risk periods.

listeningScripts.title: Workplace Safety Initiative
listeningScripts.text:
Safety Officer Tom: I've been analyzing our workplace incident reports from the past two years, and I'm concerned about our trend. We've had 34 reported injuries this year, which is up 15 percent from last year. Most incidents are slips, trips, and falls in warehouse areas. I'm proposing we implement mandatory safety training for all warehouse staff every six months, not annually as we currently do.

Warehouse Manager David: Tom, I appreciate your concern, but I'm worried about requiring training every six months. That's a lot of time away from work. My team's productivity is already under pressure with current targets. If we pull people off the floor for training frequently, we'll fall further behind on our goals. Can't we just focus on better signage and equipment?

Worker Representative Angela: I actually support Tom's proposal. I work in the warehouse, and I've seen some close calls that could have been serious. The issue isn't signage—we know the hazards. The problem is we get complacent. Regular training keeps safety top of mind. Plus, Tom, I think twice-yearly training would actually improve morale because workers feel the company cares about their wellbeing.

Safety Officer Tom: Thank you, Angela. David, I understand your concern about productivity, but consider the cost of injuries. Each workplace injury costs us about $12,000 in direct and indirect costs. If we can prevent even three injuries per year, the training pays for itself. And research shows regular safety training actually reduces injuries, which ultimately improves productivity.

listeningScripts.title: Climate Migration and Urban Planning
listeningScripts.text: Climate change is already forcing large-scale human migration, and we need to prepare for it now. Rising sea levels, extreme weather, and changing precipitation patterns are making entire regions uninhabitable. We're not just talking about future problems—this is happening today. Small island nations are literally disappearing. Coastal cities are experiencing increased flooding. Agricultural regions are becoming deserts. Where will these people go? History shows us that unplanned migration creates chaos: overcrowded cities, slums, resource conflicts, and instability. I believe cities and countries need to proactively plan for climate migration. This means developing infrastructure and housing in climate-resilient areas, creating economic opportunities for migrants, and managing population flows thoughtfully. Canada and the northern regions of other countries will likely become more desirable as climate conditions shift. Rather than letting this happen chaotically, we should be designing inclusive urban expansion, building climate-resilient communities, and preparing labor markets for population shifts. Some people see climate migration as a negative, but it's inevitable. The real question is whether we manage it responsibly or let it cause humanitarian crises. I'm advocating for proactive planning now. We should be expanding housing, infrastructure, and economic capacity in climate-safe regions. We should also help other countries adapt in place where possible. But denying this reality and refusing to plan is irresponsible.
